name: Olga Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer science. Most days I have two lectures, then I'm in the library with an AI assistant open on one side and my editor on the other. On Fridays I go to a hack night where we build silly apps till midnight. My room is in a student flat near campus, and my parents cover it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love building things fast and showing them to people. What wears me out is the pace: there's a new tool every week, and I feel guilty when I don't try it. My grades are average because I put more time into projects than into exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd tell friends the tools are still useful, they just aren't magic. Online I'd post a thread about what actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel safe. My degree stays valuable and I'm already good at the tools that do exist. The only drawback is that it'd make my side projects less special.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building. I'd finish the budgeting app I started with two friends and try to get twenty real users from the university. I'd also apply for a summer internship at a small software firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little flat. I like the energy of everyone thinking things are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI is mostly hype, does that change how you use it every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still use AI daily, because it makes me faster, not because I believe the hype. It's like a good calculator. I'd just stop pretending it will replace anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if the excitement faded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The excitement, honestly. Hack nights are fun because people believe something big is coming. If it fades, I'd still be here building, but I'd want a new reason.

say: I'd say the tools are still **useful**, just not magic.
I'd post a thread on what actually works.
think: My degree stays valuable and I'm already good with the **tools** that exist.
The main drawback is that my projects feel **less special**.
do: Finish the **budgeting app** and try to get twenty real users on campus.
Apply for a summer internship at a small **software firm**.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat without the excitement.
S0.quote: I'd still use AI daily, because it makes me faster, not because I believe the hype.
fieldNote: She uses AI daily as a **tool**, not as a belief.
Excitement and identity are tied to AI; a plateau would cost her more fun than safety.

steps.text: Finish the budgeting app with my two friends
Get twenty real users from the university
Apply for a summer internship at a small software firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and I'd be telling people to learn to use it now. But I'd also say it's not fair that companies get rich while graduates get fewer jobs. Online I'd back stronger rules and a tax on firms that replace workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit nervous. I code with AI every day, so I know how good it's getting. Juniors who only write simple code might not be needed, and that is literally my starter job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper. I'd learn how the models are built and tested, not just how to prompt them. I'd also move my side project toward something that needs judgment and users, like a tool for small local shops. I'd join the student society that talks about AI policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy in equal parts. Being near AI as it changes isn't the same as being safe from it, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own skills worry you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plain coding, because I can already see a model do my first-year exercises. The things that feel safer are choosing what to build, talking to customers, and checking if something is actually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think companies or governments should do something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Companies should hire graduates and train them, and governments should set rules and support people who lose out. I don't trust the market to fix it by itself.

say: I'd say it's **exciting**, but unfair that firms get rich while graduates get fewer jobs.
I'd back a tax on firms that replace workers.
think: I code with AI daily, so I know **how good** it's getting.
Simple junior coding, my own starter job, may **not be needed**.
do: Learn how models are built and tested, not just **prompting**.
Move my side project toward a tool for **local shops** and join the AI policy society.
S1.quote: Being near AI as it changes isn't the same as being safe from it, and I know that.
fieldNote: She sees both the **opportunity** and the threat clearly because she uses the tools.
Her answer: build judgment, customer contact and checking skills.
Progressive politics show up as tax and regulation.

steps.text: Learn how AI models are built and tested
Turn the budgeting app into a tool for local shops
Join the student society on AI policy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing in history and we're not ready. I'd stop joking about it. Online I'd demand that governments start income support and public AI before the job losses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. By 2028 AI does thinking work as well as me, and I'd have just finished second year. I might be the first group that learned to code and was never needed to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to build a real thing people use, fast, in case ownership matters more than jobs. I'd keep studying because I need the degree for something. I'd also push my parents to put money into something stable rather than shares, in case things get strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and sort of dizzy. Part of me thinks this is incredible, and part of me is scared of what it means for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what would you build or do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the shop tool, even if rough, to see if anyone pays. If it works, I'd own something instead of competing for a job. If it doesn't, at least I'd have learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be responsible if graduates can't find work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments first, and the companies that build it. A graduate can't fix a system change by trying harder. They need to be told clearly what support exists.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest thing** in history and we're not ready.
I'd demand **income support** and public AI before job losses.
think: By 2028 AI matches me, so I might be in a group that was **never needed**.
I'm frightened, but I also find it **incredible**.
do: Launch the **shop tool** quickly, even rough, to see if anyone pays.
Keep studying and ask my parents to hold money in something **stable**.
feel: **Anxious** and dizzy, thrilled and scared at once.
S2.quote: I might be the first group that learned to code and was never needed to.
fieldNote: Her adaptability turns into **action**: launch, own, test.
Anxiety is about everyone, not just herself.
Looks for ownership as a path when jobs are uncertain.

steps.text: Launch the shop tool in rough form within three months
Ask my parents to move money into something stable
Press for income support through the student policy society
Keep studying to finish the degree

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a countdown, and we should use it. I'd tell friends to build skills that stay useful beyond coding. Online I'd campaign for training funds and a reskilling right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but not scared. I'd finish my degree in 2029 and have two years of work before the AI shift. I could also save some money and keep options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work part time in a software job, and keep growing the shop tool. I'd learn security or testing, which seem harder to fully automate at first. I'd also save about a third of my allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like being told the date of an exam that you know you can't skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you a choice. Would you stay on the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because the degree is a base. With five years I can combine it with something people want, and I won't lose the thing in the rush. It's not wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from companies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hiring juniors and training them. And honesty: companies should tell staff early which jobs will change, and not just do cuts on a Friday.

say: I'd say it's a **countdown**, and we should use it.
I'd campaign for training funds and a **reskilling right**.
think: I'd finish in 2029 and get about two years of **work** first.
I could **save** money and keep my options open.
do: Finish the degree and work part time in a **software job**.
Learn **security or testing** and save a third of my allowance.
feel: **Uneasy**, like knowing the date of an exam you can't skip.
S3.quote: Companies should tell staff early which jobs will change, and not just do cuts on a Friday.
fieldNote: With time, she aims at the roles that are **harder** to automate.
Asks companies for early honesty and junior hiring.
Savings habit appears only when the timeline is clear.

steps.text: Work part time in a software job during the degree
Save a third of my allowance each month
Keep growing the shop tool with two friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good problem to have. A decade is long enough for schools, firms and governments to adjust. I'd tell people to get curious and stay curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty calm. I'd have eight years of experience when AGI arrives, and maybe my own small company. It's the version where my skills compound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish university, work for a startup, and keep building tools. I'd learn from experts in other fields, like health and law, to find real problems. I'd save steadily and maybe buy a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. Ten years is a whole second life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what is the thing you'd most like to have built?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that helps ordinary people use all this power. I'd want a free assistant for tenants or small business owners that is fair and public, not owned by one firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you still want to be in software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, yes. If thinking work gets automated, the people who know how it's built will still be needed to steer it. But I'd keep one foot in other fields.

say: I'd say it's a **good problem to have** because a decade lets everyone adjust.
think: I'd have eight years of **experience** and maybe my own small company.
This is the version where my **skills compound**.
do: Finish university, join a **startup** and keep building tools.
Learn from experts in **health and law** to find real problems.
feel: **Calm** and excited; ten years is a whole second life.
S4.quote: I'd want a free assistant for tenants or small business owners that is fair and public, not owned by one firm.
fieldNote: She is in her element with a long horizon: **building** and learning.
Dream: a public, fair assistant for tenants and small business owners.
Wants a foot in other fields, which keeps her flexible.

steps.text: Finish university and join an early-stage software startup
Build a free assistant for tenants
Learn the basics of law from a tenant advice group
Save steadily towards a small flat deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. I'd be mid-degree, my side project half built and nobody ready. What would help is public support, rules on who owns the models, and companies that keep hiring juniors and teach them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm excited about all of it. I think it's best if the people who use AI tools also have a say in the rules. I'd like to be one of those people.

headlineQuote: I think it's best if the people who use AI tools also have a say in the rules.
portrait: **Olga** is 18, studies computer science, and uses AI every day for study and for the side projects she builds with friends.
Her parents pay for her room near campus, and her average grades come from putting more time into projects.
She stays calm with a plateau or a decade, but feels anxious when the warning is only two years.
She blames firms for uneven gains, backs tax and rules, and wants to build a free assistant for tenants.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: she would be mid-degree with nothing ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Public support**, rules on who owns the models, and companies that hire and train juniors.
